bio.en: Rahul Vohra is the founder and CEO of Superhuman, the AI-powered email client, and a famously thoughtful and articulate builder who previously founded Rapportive, the first Gmail extension to scale to millions of users.
bio.zh: Rahul Vohra 是 AI 驱动电子邮件客户端 Superhuman 的创始人兼 CEO，也是一位以深思熟虑、表达清晰著称的构建者，此前曾创立首个规模化至数百万用户的 Gmail 插件 Rapportive。

summary.en: Rahul reveals that there is no such thing as a truly viral product - only word-of-mouth and remarkability - and that great products deliberately ignore much early feedback to serve a narrow, passionate wedge. He shares his 'switch log' technique for reclaiming time from calendar tyranny, his long-time Transcendental Meditation practice, and why he hired a president to offload operations. The episode is a masterclass in deliberate, taste-driven building.
summary.zh: Rahul 揭示：并不存在真正“病毒式”的产品——有的只是口碑与“值得被谈论（remarkability）”，而伟大的产品会刻意忽略大量早期反馈，只为服务一个狭窄而狂热的小切口。他分享了自己挣脱日历暴政的“切换日志（switch log）”技巧、长期的超觉冥想（TM）练习，以及为何聘请一位总裁来卸下运营重担。本期是一堂关于刻意、凭品味驱动的建设的大师课。

And then even of what they say, what do you pay attention to and what don't you? The trick here is-

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're not doing what a lot of CEOs think they need to be doing with their time. A lot of CEOs think they need to spend time on hiring or org building and you intentionally, "I will spend time on product and marketing design."
turns.zh: 你不必像许多CEO那样把时间花在招聘或组织架构搭建上，而是要刻意选择："我要把时间投入到产品和营销设计中去。"

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: This is a technique that I call the switch lock. It's born out of the observation that your calendar says what you thought you were going to do, but it's really only your trail of work that describes what you actually did. How can we capture that? So I came up with the following idea. What if I just did whatever the heck I wanted?
turns.zh: 我把这种方法称为"开关锁定法"。它源于一个观察：你的日程表显示你计划做什么，但真正能反映你实际做了什么的，只有你的工作轨迹。我们如何捕捉这一点呢？于是我想到了一个主意：那就随心所欲地做事吧！

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Hello, hello and thank you for having me Lenny.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have so many questions for you. We're going to have so much to talk about. I actually want to start with your time before Superhuman. When I was preparing for this chat, I actually asked you, what's the most pivotal moment in your career in your life? And you told me that other than starting Superhuman, it was selling your previous company Rapportive to LinkedIn. So let me just start there. What was that experience like? What do people not know about this phase in your life and just why was it so pivotal?
turns.zh: 我有很多问题想问你。我们会有很多话题要聊。实际上我想从你加入Superhuman之前的经历开始。为这次访谈做准备时，我曾问你：你职业生涯中最具决定性的时刻是什么？除了创立Superhuman，你提到还有把之前的公司Rapportive卖给LinkedIn。所以就从这儿开始吧。那段经历是怎样的？人们对那段人生经历可能不太了解，为何它如此重要？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: So for folks that don't know, Rapportive was my last company. It was the first Gmail extension to scale to millions of users. Basically on the right-hand side of Gmail, we would show you what people look like, where they work, links to their recent tweets, their LinkedIn profile and everything else that they were doing online. So if you were hiring, marketing, selling in BD, super useful. It turns out we somehow attracted most of LinkedIn's daily active users onto this one free app, and I then ultimately ended up selling that to LinkedIn. That by far, as you said, was the most pivotal thing I'd done in my career, prior to starting Superhuman. (00:06:22): Now, had I known that we'd amassed most of LinkedIn's active users onto one app, I would have sold it for far more. But the actual pivotal moment was really who I got to work with. Because I reported to LinkedIn's head of Growth, Elliot Shmukler. He was responsible for scaling LinkedIn from 25 million members to when I joined, north of 250 million members. And during my first one-on-one, I learned the real secret behind virality and big hint, it's not about viral mechanics. Overall that acquisition experience gave me the time to figure out what was next and the resources to truly swing for the fences.
turns.zh: 对于不了解的人来说，Rapportive是我上一家公司。它是首款扩展到数百万用户的Gmail插件。基本上，Gmail右侧界面会向你展示用户的外貌、工作地点、近期推特链接、LinkedIn个人资料及其他网络动态。对招聘、营销、销售和商务拓展人员来说非常实用。但最终我们不知怎的把LinkedIn的大部分日活用户都吸引到了这个免费应用上，而我最后把它卖给了LinkedIn。正如你所说，这是我在创立Superhuman之前职业生涯中最具决定性的时刻。（00:06:22）但如果当时我知道我们把LinkedIn的大部分活跃用户都吸引到了一个应用上，我本可以卖个更高的价钱。但真正关键的在于合作伙伴。当时我向LinkedIn增长部门负责人埃利奥特·施穆克勒汇报工作。他负责将LinkedIn从2500万用户扩展到我加入时的2.5亿用户。在我们的首次一对一会议上，我了解到了病毒式传播的真正秘诀——关键不在于传播机制。总之，那次收购经历让我有时间思考下一步发展，并获得了全力以赴的机会。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Well, I have to follow this thread that you put out there, what the secret is to virality. What did you learn there?
turns.zh: 好的，我得顺着你提到的病毒式传播秘诀接着问。你从中学到了什么？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Well, in my first one-on-one, I sat down with Elliot and I said, "Hey, I'm here to learn. Please teach me everything that you know about virality." And he said, "Okay. Well, hate to burst your bubble, but there is no such thing as a truly viral product." I said, "What do you mean? How do you explain Facebook for that matter? How do you explain LinkedIn?" And he said, "What I mean is, no app has sustained a viral factor of greater than one for any real period of time." Even Facebook in its heyday had a viral factor of about 0.7. And he told me that lasted for perhaps a year, so one person was creating about 0.7 new users. (00:07:57): I double-clicked again and I said, "Well Elliot, what about the address book import?" This is one of the things that LinkedIn got famous or infamous for. You could import your address book and then it would spam slash invite everyone who happens to be members of LinkedIn in your address book, and then eventually it would just invite everyone to LinkedIn. And he said, "That's an amazing feature, but you have to remember not everyone is going to use it all the time." So even that feature had a lifetime viral factor of about 0.4, and that's considered good. (00:08:28): 0.4 is good for a viral feature, 0.6 is great, something like 0.7 is absolutely incredible. You're in the stratosphere up with Facebook at that time. So I said, "Well, okay, all of these things by definition are going to Peter out. There's going to be an asymptote. None of these viral mechanics keep on compounding. Which actually makes sense, it would be a little absurd if things just kept on growing. What then is the true secret behind virality?" And he said, "It is word of mouth. It is the virality you can't measure that isn't a mechanic that isn't in a feature. It is when one user spontaneously tells another user about your product." That really colored how I think about growth and virality. Since then, it has shaped so much of what we do at Superhuman and so much of how I think about growing brands.
turns.zh: 好吧，在我第一次一对一交流时，我和埃利奥特坐下来，对他说：“嘿，我来这里是想学习的。请把你所知道的关于病毒式传播的一切都教给我。”他说：“好吧，不过我得让你失望了，根本没有所谓的真正病毒式产品。”我问：“你什么意思？那Facebook和领英又怎么解释？”他回答：“我的意思是，没有任何一款应用能在长时间内维持高于1的病毒系数。”即使是Facebook鼎盛时期，其病毒系数也仅为0.7，而且这种情况只持续了一年，即每位用户平均能带来约0.7个新用户。（00:07:57）：我又双击鼠标，问：“埃利奥特，那地址簿导入功能呢？”这正是领英成名（或声名狼藉）的原因之一。你可以导入地址簿，然后系统会向地址簿中所有领英会员发送垃圾邮件或邀请，最终所有人都被邀请加入领英。他说：“这功能很棒，但别忘了不是每个人都会一直使用它。”即便如此，该功能的终身病毒系数也仅为0.4，这已经算不错的了。（00:08:28）：0.4对于病毒式功能来说不错，0.6很棒，0.7更是令人惊叹。这已经能与Facebook相提并论了。于是我问：“好吧，那所有这些功能注定会逐渐衰退。终究会达到极限。这些病毒式机制无法持续增长。这其实说得通，如果事情一直增长下去就太荒谬了。那病毒式传播的真正秘诀是什么？” 他回答：“是口口相传。这是无法衡量的病毒式传播，不是某个功能的机制，而是用户主动向他人推荐你的产品。” 这真的改变了我对增长和病毒式传播的看法。从那以后，这一理念深刻影响了我们在Superhuman的运营，也影响了我对品牌增长的思考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, you're such a great storyteller. I'm just listening here, just captivated, "What is he going to say next?" That was fascinating. I actually have a post that I'm going to link to that, that very much aligns with what you're talking about, which is titled, Virality is a Myth mostly. It's based, I forget, on this book where they do all this research on actual viruses. It turns out they're not actually spreading in this exponential way, there's one person that spreads it to a lot of people and it keeps happening. (00:09:52): That's actually apparently what the data shows. I'm curious if you found this same thing, which is, when people think of an app as going viral, it's one person with a massive platform sharing it and their audience adopts it and that's just one to many and then it just happens a couple of times and it looks like it's going viral, but it's a person to many people, not many people to many people. Thoughts on that?
turns.zh: 哇，你真是个了不起的讲故事高手。我只是听着，被深深吸引，迫切想知道他接下来会说什么。太精彩了。实际上我有一篇帖子要分享，内容和你的观点高度契合，标题是《病毒式传播大多是个神话》。这篇文章基于一本书，里面对真实病毒进行了研究，结果发现病毒并不会以指数级传播。传播的过程是某个人把病毒传播给大量人群，然后不断重复这个过程。（00:09:52）：数据似乎确实如此。我很好奇你是否也发现了同样的现象——当人们认为某款应用“病毒式传播”时，往往是拥有巨大平台的用户分享产品，然后其受众接纳它。这就是“一个人向许多人传播”，而不是“许多人向许多人传播”。对此你有什么看法？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Yeah, we've definitely found that there are whales, to use the gaming terminology, that one person is going to be responsible for inviting 25, 50, 100 people, and they may have various motivations for doing that. In Superhuman, as an individual subscriber, if you refer somebody else and they sign up, you both get a free month, which is a great incentive if you're paying out of pocket. (00:10:39): We have people who send many, many hundreds of invites and there are some people who essentially have free Superhuman for life now due to how many people they've invited. But of course that incentive doesn't necessarily work inside of a company or inside of a team where ultimately it's the company paying for the product, so you have to then come up with new motivations for those people. That's where there really isn't any substitute to having a genuinely multiplayer or a genuinely collaborative product. That's one of the huge evolutions we've taken Superhuman through over the last, probably about two years. (00:11:15): Early last year we launched what we call Superhuman 2.0. The basic idea is, we saw almost every single other app of note become collaborative by default, Figma, Notion, Loom. These are all multiplayer or collaborative by default. Yet email, the one tool that we all use more than anything else, even more than things like Slack, was still firmly stuck in its single-player origins.
turns.zh:
是的，我们确实发现，有一些用户（用游戏术语来说）会负责邀请25人、50人、100人加入Superhuman，他们这么做可能出于各种动机。在Superhuman中，作为个人订阅用户，如果你推荐别人注册，你们双方都能获得一个月的免费体验——对于自费用户来说，这是一个极大的激励。（00:10:39）：有些人会发送数百条邀请，甚至有些人因为邀请了太多人而终身免费使用Superhuman。但这种激励机制在公司或团队内部未必适用，毕竟产品费用最终由公司承担，所以必须为这些用户找到新的激励方式。这正是Superhuman在过去两年间经历的重大进化方向。
（00:11:15）：去年年初，我们推出了Superhuman 2.0版本。核心理念是，我们发现几乎所有知名的应用（如Figma、Notion、Loom）都默认采用协作模式，而邮件——这个我们使用最频繁的工具，甚至比Slack等工具更受欢迎——却始终停留在单人使用的原始阶段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to something that you mentioned that I didn't come back to you that I think is really core to what you just shared, which is word of mouth being so important. People talk about all these viral features and sharing contact books and all these things. And your point is, that takes you to a place, but really what helps a consumer-ish product spread is word of mouth, people sharing with each other. Which, then the question is, how do you do that? We're going to talk about a lot of things that you did to make Superhuman something people want to share, but in the end it's just making something people want to share. That's the definition almost. Then it's like, what makes people want to share stuff? It's amazing, it's helping them, something that is remarkable.
turns.zh: 我想再回顾一下你提到的关键点——口碑传播的重要性。这是我们刚刚讨论的核心要素。人们总在谈论病毒式传播、通讯录共享等功能，但你强调，传播的关键在于口口相传、用户主动分享。那么如何实现这一目标呢？我们会探讨Superhuman如何打造吸引用户分享的产品，但归根结底，关键在于创造人们愿意分享的东西。这几乎就是定义所在。那么，什么能激发人们分享的欲望？答案令人惊叹——帮助他人，这才是最深刻的价值。

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Well, it turns out, because you mentioned remarkableness, that is one of our core company values. If you think about what a company has to do, it has to grow. How do things grow? Well, let's take Elliot's advice at face value, and I believe it's true, it's creating something that people share. You mentioned one way of doing it, which is something that people want to share. There's actually another way, which is simply creating something remarkable, and you used that word, and that is one of the core values of Superhuman. (00:12:53): We have, create delight, create something that is so joyful that really truly brings people delight. We have deliver remarkable quality, something that is so striking, so compelling and worthy of attention that people can't but help tell others about it. Then we have build the extraordinary, which is a measure of the efficacy or the innovativeness of what we want to build. That's another trick, which is literally baking these raw ingredients for growth into your company values.
turns.zh:
事实证明，正如你提到的“非凡性”，这正是我们公司的核心价值观之一。回想公司的使命，增长是必经之路。如何实现增长？借用Elliot的建议——创造人们愿意分享的东西。除此之外，还有另一种方法：创造非凡体验。正如你所言，这正是Superhuman的核心价值之一。
（00:12:53）：我们的价值观包括：创造惊喜，打造真正能给人带来快乐的产品；提供卓越品质，打造令人惊叹、引人入胜、值得关注的产品；打造非凡体验，衡量我们所构建产品的效用和创新能力。这是另一个秘诀——将这些增长的基本要素融入公司价值观中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I didn't know that was one of your values. That makes so much sense. Okay, we're going to come back to that, because I think that is... There's so much to learn about how you think about product and how you think about building the company that builds the product. But I want to actually start here with how this conversation came to be. (00:13:41): The CEO of Product Hunt, Rajiv, tweeted months ago, he tweeted this and we're going to show this if you're on YouTube, "Superhuman's product velocity feels like it's kicked into another gear as of late. Does anyone else notice this?" I saw that, I'm like, "I completely have noticed this. It feels like there's just feature shipping left and right, AI this, AI that. It feels like it's just a new company." And I tagged you on the tweet. I'm like, "Hey Rahul, what's changed?" And you answered with a few things and it just made it clear there's a lot to learn about what you did. (00:14:12): Because a lot of companies are in this phase of just, "Things aren't moving as fast as we want. We used to be so much faster, we used to ship all these features and now we don't." So I think this is a really cool real case study illustrative example that we can analyze. So let me ask you this, what did you notice that told you something needed to change at Superhuman? And then what did you change that actually had the most impact on your ability to ship and move faster?
turns.zh:
我之前都不知道这也是你的价值观之一。真是太有道理了。好的，我们稍后再回过头来讨论这个话题，因为我觉得这...关于你如何看待产品，以及如何打造开发产品的公司，还有太多值得学习的地方。但今天我想先从这场对话的缘起说起。（00:13:41）Product Hunt的CEO拉吉夫几个月前在推特上发了一条动态，如果你关注了YouTube的话，我们会把这条推送给你看。他写道："Superhuman最近的产品开发速度感觉又提升了一个档位。大家有没有同感？"我看到这条推文后就评论道："我完全注意到了这一点。感觉现在动不动就发布新功能，AI这个、AI那个，感觉这公司就像新创企业一样。"我还@了你，写道："嘿，拉胡尔，到底发生了什么变化？"你回复了几个关键点，这让我意识到你做了很多值得借鉴的优化。

（00:14:12）因为很多公司都处于这样一个阶段："进展没有我们期望的那么快。我们以前开发速度快得多，现在却停滞不前了。"所以我觉得Superhuman的案例非常值得研究。接下来我想问你，到底是什么让你意识到公司需要改变？然后你又做了哪些改变，才真正提升了开发效率和产品发布速度？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: I think what we noticed was this sentiment, and we felt it first ourselves, but we also started hearing it from the market, from our users, from our customers, that we'd slowed down. And as a founder, as a CEO, that's the absolute last thing you want to hear. It's our job after all to speed things up. When I ask people what do they mean by slowing down, they didn't mean the product, of course, the product wasn't working any slower, but that the pace of delivery seemed to have slowed down. (00:15:09): I think to break this down, it's important to start by defining what we mean by a slowdown. There's the kind of slowdown that is unavoidable in certain spaces, and then there is the kind of slowdown that is quite avoidable. We actually had both. So starting with unavoidable slowdown, you can classify anything that you build in a company into one of two categories, solution deepening and market widening. Now, solution deepening means making your product better for its existing users, but not making it available to more users. Whereas market widening means making your product available to more users, but not making the product itself any better. (00:15:50): There are some spaces, there are some markets, there are some platforms where market widening is really fast and really easy, and there are some spaces, email is one of them where market widening is really hard and really slow. But when we started we had a great deal of focus. We only supported Gmail, we were only on the web. In those early years, we could pour every ounce of R&D energy, every engineering dollar, into solution deepening, making the product better for existing users. And of course users loved it. It's how we got to product market fit. It's how most startups do. (00:16:24): But at a certain point, almost every company then has to start investing in widening the market. For example, the market of people who will use a new Gmail front end but without a mobile app, does exist, but it is relatively small. This is something that every new email startup is going to learn sooner or later. In order to keep on growing, you are going to have to need to add an iOS app and then a MacOS app, and then a Windows app, and then an Android app. Then you'll soon want to support Office 365. But that's not one thing, that's actually three things, because you have to support Office 365 on desktop and then on iOS and then on Android. That's all much easier said than done. (00:17:04): I think we at Superhuman now know things about these APIs that literally no other company knows, and I would not wish it upon my worst enemy. So fast-forward to today, and Superhuman now works wherever you do on every combination of Gmail, Outlook, Mac, Windows, Web, iOS, Android, and this actually turns out to be a really great technology moat. Almost no other email app can claim this. It's taken many years of intense investment. I think we'll touch on this later, but it's one of the main reasons why we can sell into the enterprise, because we now know everyone can use it. (00:17:37): But this is the hard part, when you're doing that market widening, you're not solution deepening, so your perceived product velocity may decrease. You can avoid some of these things with some smart technology decisions, but mostly you just have to grind through it, and it is worth it to get to the other side. Then there's the kind of slowdown that is avoidable. If I remember my answer to Rajiv's tweet, that was the kind I was talking about. In that case it was our management structure, or who does what. (00:18:07): When we hired our initial executive teams, I followed very conventional wisdom. I ended up with a set of VPs and eight, I think direct reports, maybe even nine. I thought that's what you were meant to do. That's how startups are meant to scale. But as anyone who's been there knows, eight direct reports is a lot. It's a lot of hiring, it's a lot of goal setting, it's a lot of OKRs, it's a lot of accountability conversations, and fortunately also it's a lot of firing. No CEO ever gets their executive team right on the first try. That time I had for the things that I think I can genuinely be world-class at things like product and design and technology and marketing, that all began to rapidly disappear, and as a result the organization began to slow down. (00:18:54): Unfortunately, I was also tracking my time very closely, I had this crazy way of tracking it. At one point I noticed I was spending six to 7% of my week on these areas, these areas where I can truly be world-class at. So I had two realizations. Number one, as CEO, once you get to a certain scale, and we were definitely at that scale, you can actually define what you want the role of a CEO to be at your company. And number two, the Superhuman opportunity deserves everyone who works at the company to spend as much time as possible in their zone of genius, so that includes me as well as everybody else. What I did is, I hired a really great president, I went from eight direct reports to two, and the amount of time that I spend on product design, technology and marketing went up from six to 7% to about 60% to 70% of my week.
turns.zh:
我认为我们注意到的是这种情绪——我们自己最先感知到了，但随后也从市场、用户和客户那里听到了反馈，称我们的发展放缓了。作为创始人和CEO，这绝对是我们最不愿听到的消息。毕竟，我们的职责就是加速前进。当我问人们所谓的"放缓"指什么时，他们当然不是指产品本身变慢了，而是交付速度似乎变慢了。（00:15:09）：要深入解析这一点，我们首先需要界定"放缓"的含义。有些放缓是某些领域不可避免的，而有些则完全可以避免。我们恰恰遇到了两者。首先是不可避免的放缓。你可以将公司开发的任何产品分为两类：解决方案深化和市场拓展。解决方案深化意味着为现有用户优化产品，而非拓展用户群体；市场拓展则意味着拓展用户群体，而非优化产品本身。（00:15:50）：有些领域、市场或平台的市场拓展速度极快且容易实现，而有些领域（如邮箱领域）则极其困难且缓慢。但我们初创时专注度极高：仅支持Gmail，仅基于网页。早期阶段，我们能将所有研发精力和工程资金投入到解决方案深化上，即优化现有用户体验。用户对此欣喜若狂，这也是我们实现产品市场匹配的关键，也是大多数初创公司的成功之道。（00:16:24）：但到了某个阶段，几乎所有公司都必须开始投资市场拓展。例如，仅支持Gmail前端但没有移动应用的用户群体确实存在，但规模相对较小。这是每个新兴邮箱初创公司迟早会面临的挑战。若想持续增长，就必须添加iOS应用、MacOS应用、Windows应用、Android应用，随后还要支持Office 365。但这并非单一任务，而是三重挑战——因为你需要在桌面端、iOS端和Android端同时支持Office 365。这说起来容易做起来难。（00:17:04）：如今的Superhuman已掌握了其他公司闻所未闻的API技术，我宁愿将这份经验送给我的死敌。快进到今天，Superhuman已能在Gmail、Outlook、Mac、Windows、网页、iOS、Android等所有平台无缝协作，这实际上构成了强大的技术护城河。几乎没有其他邮箱应用能做到这一点。这背后的投入历时多年。稍后我们会详细探讨，但这是我们能切入企业市场的核心原因——因为我们现在知道所有人都能使用它。（00:17:37）：但困难之处在于，进行市场拓展时，就无法专注于解决方案深化，因此用户感知到的产品进展速度可能会放缓。通过明智的技术决策，你或许能规避部分问题，但多数时候只能埋头苦干，但只要挺过这段时期，一切都将水到渠成。接下来是可避免的放缓。如果我记得对Rajiv推文的回复，那就是我所指的这种情况。这种情况源于我们的管理架构或权责划分。（00:18:07）：当我们聘请
刚组建初期的高管团队时，我遵循了非常传统的管理理念。最终我任命了八位副总裁（我想可能还有九位直接下属）。我以为这才是创业公司扩张的正确之道。但任何有过类似经历的人都知道，八位直接下属实在太多了。这意味着要招聘大量员工、制定无数目标、填写无数OKR、进行无数次责任追究会议——幸运的是，还要频繁解雇员工。没有哪位CEO能在第一次尝试时就组建好理想的管理团队。那些我自认为能做到世界级水准的领域——产品、设计、技术和市场营销——相关工作机会迅速消失，最终导致公司发展放缓。

（00:18:54）不幸的是，我当时还非常严格地追踪自己的时间分配，采用了一种疯狂的追踪方式。某次我发现，自己每周在这些能发挥专长的领域仅投入了6%至7%的时间。这让我意识到两点：第一，作为CEO，当公司规模达到一定阶段（而我们当时显然已经达到这个阶段），你就能明确界定CEO在公司中的角色定位。第二，Superhuman这样的公司应该让每位员工都能尽可能多地专注于自己的天赋领域——这既包括我，也包括其他所有人。于是我做出了调整：聘请了一位出色的总裁，将直接下属人数从八位缩减至两位，同时我投入在产品设计、技术和市场营销上的时间比例从6%至7%提升至每周约60%至70%。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to mirror back a few things. One is, people may feel like you are not shipping as much as you used to because you're actually building things they don't care about, which is support for office and all these things that they don't need, but the business needs to expand, integrations with Microsoft and Android and all these things. I think that's such a good point, that it looks like nothing's happening when there's a lot of good stuff happening for other users that aren't you. (00:20:15): Then there's this point about people delegate. Then a leader of delegates, hires all these execs and they're like, "This is not what I wanted. Why have I done this?" And you think it's going to speed up, but it slows down. A couple threads here that are really interesting. One is this time tracking thing, I need to know how do you do this? The fact that you knew seven to 8% or whatever the number is, to that granularity of your time you're spending on things you wanted was that low, how do you do time tracking? Let's not go super far, but just what's your approach?
turns.zh:
接下来，我想反思几点问题。首先，人们可能会觉得你现在不像过去那样积极进取了，因为你实际上在开发一些他们并不关心的功能，比如Office支持和其他无关痛痒的模块。虽然业务需要扩展，整合微软和安卓等平台也很重要，但这些对用户来说并非刚需。这种"看似无所作为"的状态，实则为其他用户带来了诸多实质性改进，这一点很值得深思。

（00:20:15）接下来是关于权力下放的问题。有些领导者委派了大量高管后，却发现"这根本不是我想要的"、"我为什么要这么做？"原本以为能加速进程，结果却适得其反。这里有几个很有意思的讨论点：比如时间追踪功能，我想知道你们是怎么做到的？你们能精确到7%-8%来追踪个人时间分配，这么细致的数据是怎么收集的？别聊太深奥的技术细节，就说说你们的具体做法吧？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: This is a technique that I call the Switch log. It's born out of the observation that your calendar says what you thought you were going to do, but it's really only your trail of work that describes what you actually did. So how can we capture that? And actually, how can we create a system of work that isn't tethered to a calendar, where you aren't at the behest of what some timetable says you do or you don't have to do? So I came up with the following idea, what if I just did whatever the heck I wanted? What if every single time I change task I just Slack DM'd my EA, but this also works in Slackbot, it just has to go somewhere. I Slack DM'd my EA and I said, "TS:," and then a few words for the task I was doing. (00:21:45): Well, that would create certain changes. Instead of having to constantly look at the calendar and think, "Oh, should I stop this task, start that task, I can just do what I want." If what I feel right now is, "Oh boy, I really need to prepare for Lenny's podcast, I'll go ahead and do that." And if I get bored or distracted eight minutes in, which sometimes happens because something else just bubbles up to the top of my mind, well, there's a reason that my body is bubbling it up to the top of my mind. I also practice transcendental meditation, so I'm very keen on the idea of being aware and listening to what's bubbling up. (00:22:20): So it's okay for me to then go and attend to that thought as opposed to start to expend my focus points or my discipline or willpower on the thing that I thought I was meant to be doing. All I'd have to do is I'd go back to Slack, "TS: Dealing with this other thing." And by the way, you should obviously turn up for your meetings. I'm not saying just blow through your meetings and not turn up for your one-on-ones. Definitely do those things. What I'm saying is, do what feels right for as long as it feels right to do. Then at the end of the week you can see where your time is going. (00:22:55): I realized at one point that I was spending only in those days 5% of my time on recruiting, whereas perhaps I should be spending 20 or 30% or more of my time on recruiting. But the biggest thing was, I saw I was only spending six to 7% of my time on product, on design, on technology and marketing. These are things where I know I'm really good at them. I should either be teaching people how to do them or doing them or some combination of both. That's probably the best thing for me. It keeps me really happy, very joyful, it keeps me sharp, but it's also scaling the organization. So that's how we had that kind of an insight. Once you have this Slack Log, you can then graph it and chart it and see where your time is actually going.
turns.zh: 这是一种我称之为"切换日志"的技巧。它源于一个观察：你的日历记录了你原本计划要做的事，但真正能体现你实际完成工作的只有你的工作记录。那么，我们如何捕捉这些信息呢？实际上，如何创建一个不受日历约束的工作系统呢？你不必受制于某个时间表规定你该做什么或不该做什么。于是我产生了这样一个想法：如果我只做我想做的事呢？每次切换任务时，我就在Slack上给我的行政助理发消息告知当前任务。（00:21:45）这样做会带来一些变化。无需不断查看日历，思考"我该停止这个任务，开始那个任务吗？"你只需顺从自己的感觉。比如现在我想，"天哪，我真的需要为Lenny的播客做准备，我要去做了。"如果八分钟后我感到无聊或分心——有时确实会这样，因为脑海中突然冒出其他想法——但身体让这些想法浮出脑海是有原因的。我还练习过超觉冥想，所以我非常重视保持觉察，倾听内心涌现的声音。（00:22:20）这样做没问题，我可以去处理这些想法，而不是把注意力和自律力浪费在本该做的事上。只需回到Slack，写道"TS：处理其他事务。"当然，你还是应该参加会议。我不是说可以逃避会议或一对一交流，而是要在感觉正确的时候做正确的事。周末结束后，你就能看到时间都花在了哪里。（00:22:55）我曾意识到，那些天我只有5%的时间用于招聘，而我本该投入20%、30%甚至更多时间。但最重要的是，我发现自己只有6%到7%的时间用于产品、设计、技术和市场营销。这些都是我擅长的领域。我应该教别人如何做这些事，或者亲自参与其中，或者两者结合。这对我来说是最好的选择。它让我快乐、充实，还能助力公司发展。这就是我们获得这种洞察的关键。一旦有了Slack日志，你就可以将其可视化分析，清楚时间都去哪儿了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How cool. Clearly this is an app opportunity or an agent opportunity where you're just telling this thing every time. It's essentially tracking context, which we're always hearing, try not to avoid context which switches.
turns.zh: 太酷了。显然这是一个应用程序或代理服务的机会，你只需每次都把这些信息告知对方。实质上是在追踪上下文转换，我们总听说要避免上下文切换。

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: I think context switches are fine. There's definitely this idea that, for every interruption you have, the brain does take roughly 21 minutes on average to recover, to get back to the efficacy before that you were disturbed. It's a big deal, of course, I'm building productivity software, we designed Superhuman to minimize the amount of distraction and disruption that's possible within the app. But if you are working on something and at the back of your mind something bubbles up, you have to attend to it in one way or the other. Sometimes I just write it down, actually, I don't have my notebook with me, but it's really big. I have a gigantic, whatever twice the size of A4 is, I guess A3 sketchbook and I always have a 4H pencil, so whenever one of those thoughts comes up, I just scribble it down. Or I actually stop what I'm doing and I attend to that task, because there's a reason it's bubbling up right now.
turns.zh: 我觉得上下文切换没关系。确实有一种说法是，每次被打断后，大脑平均需要21分钟才能恢复到被打断前的效率。这当然很重要，毕竟我开发的是生产力软件，我们设计Superhuman就是为了尽可能减少应用内可能出现的干扰和打断。但如果你正在做某件事，而脑海中突然冒出一个想法，你总得以某种方式处理它。有时我会直接把它写下来，其实我现在没带笔记本，但我有本超大的素描本，差不多A4纸的两倍大，我总带着4H铅笔。每当这种想法冒出来时，我就快速记下来。或者我会停下手头的事，专注处理那个任务，因为它此刻冒出来是有原因的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you know exactly the type of paper and pencil, 4H pencil, A3 paper, [inaudible 00:24:51]. Okay, this is going to be a theme. You mentioned meditation, you said you do TM, so you do 20 minutes in the morning, 20 minutes... Do you do it that style or you do a longer session?
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你对纸笔的精确选择，4H铅笔、A3纸，[00:24:51听不清]。好吧，这会成为一个主题。你提到了冥想，说自己练习过TM（超觉静坐），早上20分钟，下午20分钟……你是坚持这种模式，还是会延长时长？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: I do about half an hour in the morning, including rest time. The physical rest component of it is very important to me. So it's 20 minutes of the actual meditation, then 10 minutes of rest. I do that in the morning as well as in the afternoon at around 3:00 PM
turns.zh: 我早上会练半小时，包括休息时间。对我来说，实际冥想20分钟，休息10分钟。这两个时段我上午和下午都会坚持，下午大概3点左右。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you just carve that out in your calendar. Everyone knows Rahul at three o'clock, he's going to be out.
turns.zh: 你直接在日历上安排好了。大家都知道，下午3点拉胡尔要开会。

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Absolutely. My EA knows, they're the one who's organizing the calendar and making sure things happen when they need to happen. They also know that nothing can override this TM block. Without it I genuinely start to fall apart. But with it, I'm able to access some very deep competencies that I didn't have before. I've been doing this now for about four or five years, and initially I simply felt happier, occasionally even more euphoric coming out of a really great meditation session. But over time I found that my ability to focus was increasing. I could hold attention on something for much longer, but I also was able to become much more creative and much more expressive. (00:26:02): These are well-known side effects, as it were, or intended effects for some people of TM. And interestingly about TM, if you compare it to other forms of meditation, they don't have quite the same impact across quite as many executive functions. So there's something particularly interesting that's going on with transcendental meditation as opposed to other forms that folks are still trying to unravel and figure out.
turns.zh: 当然。我助理知道这些，他们负责日程安排，确保事务按时进行。他们也知道TM练习时间不可被打断。没有它，我真的会崩溃。但有了它，我能激发一些从前没有的深层能力。坚持四五年后，我发现专注力明显增强，能更久地专注于一件事，也更具创造力和表达力了。（00:26:02）：这些都是众所周知的副作用，或者说对某些人是预期效果。有趣的是，与其他冥想形式相比，TM对多个执行功能的影响更显著。这说明相较于其他冥想方式，超觉静坐存在一些独特的机制，人们至今仍在探索其奥秘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If folks want to, if they're inspired and they want to check out this form of meditation, any advice on where they could go learn?
turns.zh: 如果有人感兴趣，想要尝试这种冥想，有什么推荐的学习资源吗？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Absolutely, a lot. But in summary, have a coach teach you. I had many false starts myself with meditation, trying the various apps, learning from books. None of it really worked for me. What worked was having one-on-one teaching from someone themselves who had been taught one-on-one the Yogic or the Raja tradition of teaching. This person in particular had also been a venture-backed founder multiple times over, so they're very well aware of the kinds of stresses that I tend to be under. And all of his clients are mostly in technology as well. If you're in the Bay Area, this person's name is Laurent Valasek. They run an institution called the Peak Leadership Institute. And this is all about how we can live a more integrated and whole life. Integrating wellness practices like meditation, but for the purpose of unlocking peak performance in life and in business.
turns.zh: 确实，遇到过很多挑战。但总的来说，我建议找一位教练来指导你。我自己在冥想方面也走过不少弯路，尝试过各种应用程序，研读过相关书籍，但效果都不理想。真正对我有效的，是接受一对一教学——由那些曾接受过一对一传统瑜伽或王室教学法训练的人亲自授课。这位教练还曾多次成功创办获得风投支持的公司，因此他深知我所承受的各种压力。他的客户大多来自科技领域。如果你在湾区，这位教练叫劳伦特·瓦拉塞克（Laurent Valasek），他经营着一家名为"巅峰领导力研究所"的机构。核心理念是如何过上更完整、更融合的生活，融合诸如冥想等健康实践，最终释放个人及事业的巅峰表现力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thank you for sharing that. That is very actionable. We're going to link to that in the show notes. (00:27:35): Okay. I'm going to try to bring us back on course. The other thing you mentioned that I think is really interesting is hiring a president. A lot of founders and leaders might be hearing this and be like, "Going from eight reports and doing all these things I don't want to, spending most of my time on the product and design and marketing, amazing." What did this president take off your plate and what is their responsibility and that allowed you to do the stuff you wanted to do?
turns.zh: 感谢分享这些见解。这非常实用。我们会把相关链接放在节目笔记里。（00:27:35）：好的，我来把话题拉回正轨。你提到的聘请总裁这件事，我觉得特别有意思。很多创始人和领导者听到这个建议，可能觉得：“从八项汇报中解脱出来，做自己想做的事，专注产品、设计和营销，太棒了。” 那总裁具体为你分担了哪些工作，承担了哪些责任，又如何让你得以专注于自己想做的事？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: The biggest thing was taking off the operations and the management of the executive team and the rest of the company. Think of the president role in Superhuman as an operationally extremely challenging and a very growthful role. It is perfect for someone who wants to go on to be a CEO in their next role. Instead of hiring and firing that team, instead of managing and setting their goals, instead of the accountability conversations, someone else who's now doing that. (00:28:35): In addition, because that's not the only job, in addition, they're also a very strong thought partner when it comes to corporate strategy. When it comes to, where do we take act one, our email product? How far do we go down the multiplayer path? How aggressively should we lean into AI? What's a reasonable gross margin in a world with AI? Are we from a financial perspective okay dipping now and then coming back later? When should we start building our second product? How do we think about our R&D strategy? Should we keep on hiring in the Bay Area, or as we've done for many of our recent hires, should we continue hiring in Latin America? Should we consider other time zones as well? And so on and so on and so on. I'm just randomly coming up with questions, but the list is truly endless. (00:29:27): Another way to think about it is, it's almost like a grown-up co-founder. The two people I co-founded the company with, Comrade and Vivek, they've long since gone from Superhuman. We're now a 10-year-old organization and I'm one those rare founders that is persisting and thriving actually 10 years in. That said, the journey never gets easier, it gets different and you still need that co-founding energy around you. I have a handful of people in the organization who are in their roles providing that kind of energy, that kind of input, and who thrive off doing so. Then the president role is definitely one of them.
turns.zh: 最重要的是，他接手了运营和管理高管团队及整个公司的工作。可以把Superhuman中的总裁角色视为一个极具挑战性、又能助力成长的职位。这对那些渴望未来晋升CEO的人来说，再合适不过了。总裁不再需要亲自招聘和解雇团队，不用亲自设定目标，不用进行责任追究，现在这些事由他人代劳。（00:28:35）：此外，这份工作不止于此。总裁还是企业战略方面的得力智囊。比如：我们要如何推进第一阶段的邮件产品？在多人游戏路线上，我们该走多远？在AI领域，我们该如何大胆布局？在AI时代，合理的毛利率应该是多少？从财务角度看，我们现在该不该小规模投入，再回头？何时该着手开发第二款产品？如何规划研发战略？是继续在湾区招人？还是像近期许多招聘那样，转向拉丁美洲？是否还要考虑其他时区？诸如此类的问题层出不穷。（00:29:27）：换个角度看，这就像一个成熟的联合创始人。与我共同创办Superhuman的两位伙伴，Comrade和Vivek早已离开公司。如今Superhuman已走过十年历程，我是为数不多坚持并持续成功的创始人之一。但这条路从未变得轻松，只是形式变了。你依然需要那种创业伙伴的能量。在公司里，我有几位成员能提供这样的能量、见解，并乐在其中。总裁这个角色，无疑是其中之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Incredibly interesting. There's so much there. One, just a couple of things I'll share and then I want to move on to a different topic. One is just, it's cool the solution to helping you move faster and do the work you want to do is org design. That feels like a really doable thing. If you're finding you're not spending time on things you want to spend time on and things aren't moving as fast as you want, it's essentially you can find people to take on things that you don't want and shift the way that the org is structured and that could solve a lot of problems. That's what it did for you. Then I think it's also really interesting, there's this lesson here of as a founder, if you're just feeling depleted or just don't have the partner you want, you could bring someone on that could be that person.
turns.zh: 真是太有趣了。内容实在太多了。我只想分享几点，然后再转到另一个话题。首先，组织设计能帮助你提高工作效率、完成想做的事，这点太酷了。这感觉是个切实可行的方案。如果你发现自己没有把时间花在想做的事上，工作进展又不尽如人意，关键在于找人接手你不愿做的事，调整组织架构，这样就能解决很多问题。Superhuman的创始人Ed Sims就是这么做的。

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. There's so much there. That was much more of a rich area than I even expected. I want to zoom out a little bit, and there's a couple themes that came up again and again when I talked to folks that you've worked with, investors in Superhuman. The two themes are contrarian thinking, in terms of building the company, and strong attention to detail. Let's spend a little time on attention to detail. Like I said, this is one of the things that came up again and again when I was asking people about you. So I have this quote from Ed Sims, and maybe your first investor. Were they your first investor?
turns.zh: 好的，内容实在太丰富了，远超我的预期。我想稍微回顾一下，和Superhuman的投资者们交流时，反复提到的两个主题：一是逆向思维，另一是注重细节。先说细节部分。正如我所说，当我询问别人对你的看法时，这个话题反复出现。以下是Ed Sims（或许是你的首位投资者）的原话：

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Yeah, that there's a bunch of people on Twitter who are going to fight for that. But to set the record straight, Ed Sim did actually write the first three checks into Superhuman.
turns.zh: 对啊，有很多人在推特上为此争论不休。但澄清一下，Ed Sim确实为Superhuman写了前三张支票。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First three checks? At subsequent rounds.
turns.zh: 前三张支票？后续轮次的。

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Well, yeah. Quick sidebar on that, he runs Boldstart Ventures alongside his partner Elliot Durbin. They have a particular interest in backing second-time founders, but they'll also back first-time founders, and they love application and infrastructure areas like Superhuman, so we were like the perfect investment. He also wrote a check from his previous fund into a Rapportive, and I think I'd made him five X that money. Nothing to write home about, but definitely, "I'm going to back this guy again." So I went to him and I said, "Hey listen, this is going to sound crazy. I want to take on Gmail." He said, "Do you have a deck?" I was like, "Yeah, here it is one slide, here it is." And there was a screenshot of Gmail with most of it scribbled out, "I want to build that and it's going to be amazing." (00:32:25): So he said, "Cool, we're in. Can I wire you the money?" And I said, "No, I don't even have a bank account yet." I come back two days later with a bank account and he's like, "Cool, I want to wire you 750 K." And I said, "I don't even know what I'm going to do with that money. I'm not paying myself, I won't for a while. We don't have any employees. I can't think of anything I want to spend it on. Tell you what, I'll just take 250 K." And he was like, "What?" I'm like, "Yeah, I'll just take 250 K." We start having the conversation around venture economics. I'm like, "Yeah, it's fine, we'll figure it out." Then a few months back I took another 250 K and a few months back I took another 250 K as I began inventing ways and finding channels to deploy capital properly.
turns.zh: 嗯，对。顺便说一下，他和合伙人Elliot Durbin共同经营Boldstart Ventures。他们特别关注二次创业者，但也会支持初次创业者，而且对Superhuman这类应用和基础设施领域情有独钟。我们堪称完美投资案例。他还从前一个基金投了Rapportive的钱，我记得我为他赚了五倍回报。虽然不算惊人，但确实让他下定决心再支持我一次。所以我去找他说："嘿，听着，这个想法可能听起来很疯狂。我想挑战Gmail。"他问："你有演示文稿吗？"我说："有啊，就一张幻灯片。"然后是Gmail的截图，大部分都被涂掉了，写着："我想开发这个，肯定超棒的。"（00:32:25）他说："好的，我们入股。我能转账吗？"我说："不行，我还没开银行账户呢。" 两天后我开好账户，他说："那好，转75万。" 我说："我都不知道这钱怎么用。我短期内不会给自己发工资，也没员工。我想不到用处。要不你先转25万吧。" 他说："什么？" 我说："对，就25万吧。" 之后我们开始讨论风险投资经济学。我说："没关系，我们会想办法的。" 几个月前我又拿了25万，再几个月前又拿了25万，期间我一直在想办法合理配置资金。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this story. I love all these stories you're sharing I've never heard before. And by the way, it is awesome. We're talking about him coming on the podcast, maybe breaking our VC rule. So specifically the story he shared with me that is maybe an example of you and your attention to detail is, he said that you created your own font because existing fonts weren't good enough. Is that true?
turns.zh: 我超爱这个故事。你们分享的这些我从未听过的故事都太棒了。对了，我们正在讨论他来做客播客的事，说不定还能打破我们不邀请风投的规矩。具体来说，他跟我分享的那个故事，或许能体现你对细节的关注。他说你专门设计了自己的字体，因为市面上的字体都不够好。这是真的吗？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Kind of. Okay. The font that we use today is a modified version of Adelle Sans. The story there is, I looked at all of the major font families, and honestly none of them was what I would call truly excellent. That may sound like an odd thing to say. So let's, if you will permit me to talk about typography and email-
turns.zh: 算是吧。这字体是我们现在用的Adelle Sans的改良版。当时我研究了所有主流字体系列，坦白说，没有一个能称得上真正出色。这听起来可能有点奇怪。既然你们允许我聊聊排版和邮件设计——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Please.
turns.zh: 麻烦了。

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: The first thing we did was, we took our UI and we laid it out in about 15 different styles using examples of the major font families. We actually printed these out and we left them on a desk in the middle of our office. Sometimes with design, you want to tune in to your immediate most visceral response, but sometimes you want to truly let a design marinate. And this was the latter. So we let these designs marinate, we let these font choices percolate. Like I said, none of them was truly excellent. (00:34:31): Number one, I was looking for a font that was in and of itself gorgeous. Number two, I was looking for a font that could also convey a message of any kind, without overpowering the sentiment of that message. For example, does the font work when this is inviting you to a party? Many fonts, including almost all serif fonts, are actually too somber or too sober for that. Or to pick another extreme, does the font work if it is informing you of somebody's passing, many fonts are just too jaunty for that. You wouldn't want that kind of message in Comic Sans, for example. And number three, I was optimizing for a font that made reading speed and comprehension really fast. And number four, I was looking for a font that made email addresses themselves look great. So I discarded all the 15 because they weren't good enough, and after searching high and low, I came across a font called Adelle Sans, which is designed by a foundry called Type Together, type-together.com. They have a whole bunch of lovely fonts, go check them out. (00:35:36): And if you go through my list, number one, Adelle Sans is gorgeous. I think each character is a work of art. It's beautifully formed. Number two, Adelle Sans is, I would say upbeat, it's optimistic, yet it's serious enough to convey any kind of message. It has just the right amount of personality, yet not too much personality. Number three, Adelle Sans is also unusually narrow, and that actually fits email particularly well. One of my pet peeves with Gmail, which by default uses Ariel, is that the lines are as wide as your window. So if you're in a wide screen, then the lines get really arbitrarily long. The problem with really wide and really long lines, is that they decrease reading speed. Because by the time you've reached the end of one line, your eyes have lost track of the start of the next line. And Ariel itself has fairly wide characters, which further exacerbates that. (00:36:30): So at Superhuman we, if you've used the product, you know this, we fix the line length or the typographical measure to the optimal length for reading speed, which depending on the font is around 90 to 120 characters. And Adelle Sans is quite narrow, so it actually lets us do this on quite small windows with fairly dense line. So we get a lot of information on fairly small windows without getting a very long typographical measure, optimizing for reading speed and for comprehension. Then number four, finally Adelle Sans has very unusual treatment of the at symbol in an email address. It actually puts the base of the A in the at on the same baseline as the rest of the text. (00:37:15): So for example, if your name has an A, my name does Rahul at Vohra, three A's and or two A's and an at, they're all actually on the same baseline. It's a small thing, but it makes the email addresses look incredibly natural. If you look at that and then you actually look at email addresses laid out in other fonts, those other the fonts look really clunky and awkward because the A is kind of shifted around and it just looks a bit silly in my opinion. Now Adelle Sans isn't perfect. So we then worked with a type designer on some of the specific details that there are some of the glyphs, which get a little pinchy as it were, and what we use today is very close to retail Adelle Sans.
turns.zh:
我们的首要任务是，将现有的用户界面（UI）设计以约15种不同风格进行排版，并选取主流字体家族的示例进行展示。我们把这些设计稿打印出来，放在办公室中央的桌子上。有时候在设计过程中，我们需要紧紧抓住最直观的本能反应，但有时也需要让设计方案充分沉淀。这一次，我们选择了后者。因此，我们让这些设计方案静置沉淀，让字体选择逐渐浮出水面。我说过，没有一个设计是完美无缺的。（00:34:31）  
第一，我寻找的是本身就极具美感的字体。第二，我希望字体能传达任何类型的信息，同时不压盖原文的情感色彩。例如，当邀请他人参加派对时，字体是否合适？许多字体（包括几乎所有衬线字体）都显得过于庄重或冷淡。再举个极端例子，若要告知某人去世的消息，多数字体又过于轻快。例如，Comic Sans字体就不适合这种场合。第三，我致力于优化阅读速度，确保信息易于理解。第四，我要让邮箱地址本身看起来美观。  
最终，我从15种字体中筛选出Adelle Sans。这款字体由Type Together（type-together.com）设计的字体库打造，他们拥有一系列精美的字体，值得一探。  
（00:35:36）  
从我的评测来看：  
第一，Adelle Sans极具美感。我认为每个字符都是艺术品，形态优美。  
第二，Adelle Sans充满活力与乐观，又足够严谨，传达任何信息时都恰到好处。它恰如其分地展现了个性，又不过分张扬。  
第三，Adelle Sans字体较窄，尤其适合邮箱设计。我对Gmail默认字体Ariel的槽点之一是字体过宽，导致在宽屏下行过长。过宽过长的行距会降低阅读速度，因为等你读完一行字，视线已追不上下一行。Ariel本身字符宽度也偏大，加剧了这个问题。  
（00:36:30）  
在Superhuman，我们深知这一问题——如果你使用过我们的产品，就会发现我们会将行距调整至最优阅读范围，通常为90至120个字符。Adelle Sans字体较窄，因此即使在小窗口中也能呈现高密度内容，同时保持阅读流畅。  
第四，Adelle Sans在邮箱地址中的@符号处理极为巧妙。它将A的基线与其他文本对齐。  
（00:37:15）  
举例来说，如果你的名字中含三个A（如Rahul@Vohra），两个A和一个@符号，这些字符在Adelle Sans中都处于同一基线。这虽是细微之处，但却让邮箱地址显得自然流畅。对比其他字体设计，A字符位置错乱，整体显得生硬笨拙。
没有意见。现在，Adelle Sans 字体并不完美。因此，我们与字体设计师合作，对一些具体细节进行了优化，比如某些字符形状有些生硬。不过我们现在使用的版本已经与市售的 Adelle Sans 字体非常接近了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this was pre-launch or this was after you'd already launched?
turns.zh: 这是在产品上线前还是上线后？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: We'd probably had about 10, 15 users at the time.
turns.zh: 当时我们大概有10到15个用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I think that's pretty contrarian unique to be this focused on the font and the typeface before you even launched. This was like, "Is this even going to be a thing? Will anyone even care?" And I think this says a lot about the way you think about product.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得，在产品上线前就如此专注于字体和排版，这确实很与众不同。这就像在想：“这东西到底能不能成？会有人关心吗？”我觉得这充分说明了你对产品的思考方式。

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Oh yeah, that thought never crossed my mind. I think we'll probably come to it later, but the idea that, is this never going to be a thing? I think that's a dangerous thought. We can't start thinking that way, because at what point do you stop second-guessing yourself?
turns.zh: 哦，是啊，我从没想过这个问题。我们可能之后会考虑，但“这东西永远都不会成功吗？”这种想法很危险。我们不能有这种心态，否则什么时候才能停止自我怀疑？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So you were confident this was going to work, so because I am so confident it'll work, I need them to get this right. There's also this trap founders fall into of just spending too much time perfecting a thing that never works and there's always advice launch early, launch often. Thoughts there? How do you find that balance? What's your advice there?
turns.zh: 有意思。所以你当时很确定这个产品能成功，所以我现在也很确定它会成功，所以我需要他们把字体做好。创始人常会陷入一个误区，就是花太多时间去完善一个根本行不通的东西。总有人建议早点上线、多上线。你怎么看？如何找到平衡？你有什么建议？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: How much to spend time ahead of launch really does depend on the markets and the structure, the nature of your business model. For example, let's say you are building a marketplace in a greenfield opportunity, so imagine the Lyft or Uber in their heyday. There's a strong network effect, because the more cars you have on your platform, the shorter waiting times are, therefore people are going to preferentially use your app versus the other person's app. That's when there's no time to spare, that's when you probably shouldn't even be sleeping. You're going to hire the most aggressive maniacal people possible. You're going to work 120-hour weeks, because every marginal minute actually does matter. Every marginal minute in the market, growing compounding is going to make your next year even better. (00:39:51): That's actually not true of all startups and it certainly isn't true of something like Superhuman. Yes, working harder is always better and we work tremendously hard at Superhuman, but not to the point where it made sense to release something that didn't work. I'm reminded of a story of a founder that was in Y Combinator, told me about their demo day experience. They used Mailbox, which some folks may remember was also a startup, and Dropbox famously acquired them for about a hundred million dollars. The reason that they were well known, apart from the acquisition, is they were the first to popularize, swipe to archive or swipe to mark down, which of course is now standard in Superhuman and every other app. (00:40:43): This founder was using Mailbox and was having an amazing demo day. They're working the room, they're meeting investors, they're pitching their photography app in this case. He went home that night and went to his laptop, fired up mailbox and sent off a bunch of follow-up emails. He waited the day, didn't hear back, he waited two days, didn't hear back. On the third morning he figured something was up, so he fired up Gmail, went to his sent mail, and you guessed it, there were no sent mails there. So something had broken with mailbox. So he's cursing to himself trying to remind himself everything's going to be okay. Sent all the same emails from Gmail manually and they all came through. (00:41:37): But then one of the investors said, "Hey, by the way, you might want to check your email clients, because I've been getting some of your emails twice." Now he goes back into his Gmail, he sees that yes, actually the original emails that were queued up in mailbox have now indeed been sent, and some of the investors, and unfortunately most of the investors he actually pitched twice. Now, is this the end of the world? No, an investor can overlook that. Probably a good thing that you're trying new apps. But was it horrifying and was it really scary? Absolutely. (00:42:08): Imagine this wasn't investors, imagine this was a customer, someone who you were trying to convince to buy your thing and that you knew what you were doing and you had attention to detail and you had everything just buttoned up and under control. Well, now you've lost face, now you look foolish. That's why when you have mission-critical products like email where you are interfacing with customers, with candidates, with investors, it turns out to really matter. Email is mission-critical. It's not something where you can simply launch with a half-baked product.
turns.zh:
启动前投入多少时间确实取决于市场环境、业务模式的性质。举个例子，如果你正在一个全新的市场领域打造一个平台，就比如Lyft或Uber在鼎盛时期那样。这种情况下存在强大的网络效应——平台上的车辆越多，等待时间越短，用户就越倾向于使用你的应用而非竞争对手。这时候根本没有时间可以浪费，甚至可能连睡觉的时间都没有。你需要招聘最富有进取心、疯狂拼搏的人才，工作120小时每周，因为每一分时间都至关重要。市场上的每一分时间都在累积复利，助力你来年更上层楼。

（00:39:51）：但并非所有初创公司都适用这种模式，Superhuman显然不是。没错，更加努力总是好的，我们在Superhuman也确实如此，但绝不会为了发布一个不成熟的产品而仓促行事。让我讲个Y Combinator项目创始人的故事。他们用了Mailbox（可能有人还记得这个初创公司，Dropbox曾以约1亿美元收购）作为演示日的主打产品。Mailbox之所以闻名，除了被收购，还有一项创新——滑动归档或标记邮件的功能，如今已成为Superhuman等应用的标配。

（00:40:43）：这位创始人在Y Combinator的演示日表现出色，与投资者交流，推销自己的摄影应用。晚上回家后，他登录Mailbox发送后续邮件，但两天未获回复。第三天早上，他发现Mailbox崩溃了，发送记录消失。投资者随后反馈收到重复邮件，他才意识到问题所在，手动将邮件重新发送后才成功送达。

（00:41:37）：但其中一位投资者提醒：“你可能需要检查邮件客户端，我收到了重复邮件。”他查看，果然Mailbox的原始邮件已发送，部分投资者甚至收到了两次通知。是灾难吗？不，投资者可以理解。但这种情况确实令人心惊和尴尬。

（00:42:08）：想象如果不是投资者，而是客户——你试图说服他们购买产品，明明自己准备充分、处处精心，却出状况。这时你会颜面尽失，显得十分愚蠢。因此，邮件这类与客户、候选人、投资者直接交互的关键产品，必须精心打磨，绝不能半途而废。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is such an important nuance take on, there's always this debate, how much to focus on craft and user experience, how much to focus on time to launch and get it out and speed. What I'm hearing here, which I completely agree with is, it depends on the market you're in and the criticality essentially of your product. So if it's email, it just needs to work and you need to get that right, you need to spend all the time, you need to get that right. (00:43:03): This reminds me of something else that when your early investors shared with me, Bill Trenchard from First-Round Capital. He talked about how speed was the thing that you just dialed up as a lever to 11. That's where you just, "We will make this the focus. Speed, speed, speed." I think maybe the lesson there is, you pick the thing that you think will most differentiate you, make you significantly better than what's out there. So just thoughts on how you decided speed was the thing you were going to obsess with, and advice for folks that are trying to decide where to dial up things to 11?
turns.zh: 这是一个非常重要的细微差别。人们总是争论，应该在工艺和用户体验上投入多少精力，还是应该更关注上线速度和效率。我完全赞同这里提到的观点：这取决于你所处的市场以及产品的重要性。比如邮箱应用只需要确保功能正常，用户体验良好，因此需要投入大量时间把这部分做好。（00:43:03） 这让我想起早期投资者Bill Trenchard分享的经验。他提到，速度是可以被无限放大的核心优势。当时团队就决定把速度作为优先发展方向，专注于“速度、速度、速度”。我想，这背后有深刻的启示——你需要找到最能体现产品差异化的核心竞争力，确保其比现有同类产品更出色。那么，你是如何确定速度是需要全力攻关的方向，又能给那些正面临取舍的创业者哪些建议呢？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Bill is right and I agree with him, you have to pick something. Knowing what to pick is the trick. In the early days of Superhuman, I read a book on positioning that really influenced my thinking. It is, I believe called Positioning the Battle for Your Mind. It struck me how the most well-known brands have stood for one clear thing, they have a clear position. So in order for Superhuman to be memorable, I believed that we needed to occupy a clear position that was unique and which was available and which reinforced our product strategy. (00:44:12): In the first year of Superhuman, therefore, I interviewed hundreds of potential customers about their experience with Gmail and with Outlook. And predictably, almost everybody says that email takes way too much time. But interestingly, many people also said that Gmail and Outlook were way too slow. That was how I first thought that speed could be an interesting position for us. I then asked myself, "Is the position of speed unique and is it available?" And the answer was overwhelmingly yes, because almost no software was being sold or has ever been sold on the value proposition of speed. The last time I could remember anyone trying to do this, was when Google launched Chrome, and obviously that went incredibly well for them. You may remember they had slow-motion videos where they were comparing Chrome render webpages and showing that was faster than an actual strike of lightning. No one had done it since then. (00:45:15): I then asked, "Well, does speed reinforce our product strategy?" And again, the answer was overwhelmingly yes. I knew that our competition was not going to be startups, it was incumbents. And I also knew that incumbents generally struggle with speed, because by definition they have massive scale and usually entrenched architecture. Then finally I did what I call the cocktail party test, which is to look at the cocktail parties and to watch how people pitch your product to other people. In our case the pitches were simple. People would say, "Dude, you have to use it, it's really fucking fast." And that's it. That was the pitch. That's how I knew that speed would be a really great position for us to start with.
turns.zh:
Bill说得对，我完全赞同他的观点。关键在于如何选定方向。Superhuman早期，我读了一本定位理论书籍《定位：心智占领术》，深受启发。书中指出，最成功的品牌都坚持一个清晰的定位。因此，Superhuman要想脱颖而出，就必须占据一个独特、易于传播且与产品战略相契合的定位。（00:44:12）  
为此，Superhuman成立首年，我采访了数百位潜在用户，了解他们对Gmail和Outlook的使用体验。不出所料，几乎所有人都抱怨邮件耗时过长。但有趣的是，许多人也认为Gmail和Outlook速度太慢。这让我意识到，速度或许是我们的突破口。接着我自问：速度定位是否独特且可行？答案是肯定的，因为几乎没有软件以速度为核心卖点。上一次类似尝试是谷歌推出Chrome浏览器，显然取得了巨大成功。（00:45:15）  
最后我反思：速度是否能强化产品战略？答案同样肯定。我深知我们的竞争对手不是初创公司，而是行业巨头。而这些巨头往往在速度上存在天然劣势——规模庞大且架构固化。最后，通过“鸡尾酒会测试”验证定位：用户只需简单一句“兄弟，你必须用这个，速度快得离谱”。这就是我确定速度是首要定位的依据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to chat with Christina Gilbert, the founder of OneSchema, one of our longtime podcast sponsors. Hi Christina.
turns.zh: 很高兴与OneSchema创始人Christina Gilbert交流，她是我们播客的长期赞助商之一。Christina，你好。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Yes, thank you for having me on, Lenny.
turns.zh: 是的，感谢你邀请我参加节目，Lenny。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is the latest with OneSchema? I know you now work with some of my favorite companies like Ramp, Vanta, Scale and Watershed. I heard that you just launched a new product to help product teams import CSVs from especially tricky systems like ERPs.
turns.zh: OneSchema的最新进展如何？我知道你现在与Ramp、Vanta、Scale和Watershed等我最喜欢的公司合作。我听说你们刚刚推出了一个新产品，帮助产品团队从ERP等特别复杂的系统导入CSV数据。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Yes, so we just launched OneSchema of FileFeeds, which allows you to build an integration with any system in 15 minutes, as long as you can export a CSV to an SFTP folder. We see our customers all the time getting stuck with hacks and workarounds, and the product teams that we work with don't have to turn down prospects because their systems are too hard to integrate with. We allow our customers to offer thousands of integrations without involving their engineering team at all.
turns.zh: 是的，我们刚刚推出了FileFeeds的OneSchema，只要你能将CSV导出到SFTP文件夹，就能在15分钟内与任何系统建立集成。我们经常看到客户深陷于临时解决方案的困境，而与我们合作的产品团队无需因系统难以集成而拒绝潜在客户。我们让客户无需动用工程团队即可提供数千种集成服务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can tell you that if my team had to build integrations like this, how nice would it be to be able to take this off my roadmap and instead use something like OneSchema. Not just to build it but also to maintain it forever.
turns.zh: 我可以告诉你，如果我的团队要自己开发这样的集成功能，能用OneSchema这样的工具替代现有方案该有多好啊。不仅能节省开发时间，还能实现长期维护。

turns.speaker: Christina Gilbert
turns.en: Absolutely, Lenny. We've heard so many horror stories of multi-day outages from even just a handful of bad records. We are laser focused on integration reliability to help teams end all of those distractions that come up with integrations. We have a built-in validation layer that stops any bad data from entering your system and OneSchema will notify your team immediately of any data that looks incorrect.
turns.zh: 确实如此，Lenny。我们听过太多因为少数错误记录导致数日停机的恐怖故事。我们致力于提升集成可靠性，帮助团队消除集成带来的各种干扰。我们内置的验证层能阻止错误数据进入系统，一旦发现数据异常，OneSchema会立即通知团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I know that importing incorrect data can cause all kinds of pain for your customers and quickly lose their trust. Christina, thank you for joining us and if you want to learn more, head on over to OneSchema.co. That's one OneSchema.co. (00:47:33): The next area I want to spend time on and I imagine we'll have much insight is, some of the contrarian ways you approach building Superhuman that a lot of companies never thought about doing that you did that worked out for you. So the first is manually onboarding every single new user. Sure, startups have done this, founders bring on some folks and then cool, show it to them and then they stop doing that and then it's self-service or sales teams. How far did you scale this manual onboarding phase of your company? How many people did you have onboarding people, how many people did you manually onboard?
turns.zh: 我知道导入错误数据会让客户失去信任，信任危机转瞬即至。Christina，感谢你加入我们的节目。如果想了解更多信息，请访问OneSchema.co。（00:47:33）：接下来我想探讨的是你们在构建Superhuman时采取的一些反常规方法，这些方法许多公司从未想过，却在你们这里奏效了。首先是手动为每个新用户进行入职培训。当然，初创公司也这么做过，创始人招来几个人培训一遍，然后就放手让用户自助操作，或者交给销售团队。你们公司手动入职培训阶段规模有多大？有多少人负责入职培训，又有多少用户是手动入职的？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: So for folks that don't know, in those early days we insisted on one-to-one concierge onboarding, and it was absolutely the right thing to do. You couldn't use Superhuman unless you went through the onboarding experience. Now it's almost the reverse. Almost every new Superhuman customer goes through self-service. The onboarding experience is still there, but again it is absolutely the right thing to do. To answer your question, at peak we had about 20 people doing manual onboarding.
turns.zh: 早期我们坚持一对一的专属入职服务，这绝对是正确的做法。没有完成入职流程就无法使用Superhuman。现在情况几乎反过来了。几乎每个新用户都是自助入职。不过入职体验依然保留，这也是正确的做法。回答你的问题，最高峰时我们有20人负责手动入职。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so it's not that many people. That's really interesting. Because I always imagined it was like a massive team, but 20 people can handle a lot, is the takeaway there. What was the scale where you stopped manual onboarding, just for folks that are thinking about doing this and then when to stop?
turns.zh: 好的，人数不算多。这真的很有趣。我一直以为会是个庞大的团队，但20人也能处理不少业务，值得借鉴。你们停止手动入职的规模是多少？对于考虑采取这种做法的人来说，什么时候该停止？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: I think the reason to stop is that there will always be certain personality types who do not want to go through a one-on-one onboarding. At a certain point those people will become very important, and you'll need to be ready with a world-class self-service option. When we started building self-service, it seemed nearly impossible. In fact, it was terrifying, because it's difficult to overstate how much the entire DNA of the company was built around this idea that we would onboard users manually. After all, we did so much in our one-to-one onboardings and there's only so much that software can do. Now, we did after a lot of grind and persistence eventually figure it out and we have a world-class self-service experience today, but we did not at the time. (00:49:49): So the flip side is, why would you even do this to begin with? What we found is two things. Number one, the user metrics are excellent for things like engagement, retention, product market fit score, MPS, virality, for all of those metrics. I think you you'll significantly beat your industry benchmarks if you go to the effort of one-on-one onboarding your early customers. It becomes so powerful to have that early cohort of super fans when it comes to things like building a brand. If folks remember that conversation from way up at the top, what is it that creates true virality? It's not viral mechanics, it's word of mouth. It is brand. This is how you can kickstart a brand. (00:50:32): And number two, in a world where you can easily and quickly raise funding, like for example the zero interest rate phenomenon era, you can actually use dollars to avoid building a first-time user experience and all of the normal growth loops that you would then have to build. You would then instead focus all of your engineers on finding product market fit or in solution deepening or in market widening, but not for example on a first-time user experience, not for example on activation, because you have humans doing activation for you. By contrast I saw other companies often competing spend almost half their engineering dollars on those things, on self-service flows for products that ultimately did not find products market fit. So makes sense to do if you really want to create that brand, which I think all consumer-ish companies need to do. And if there is money falling off trees, for whatever reason, which we did have for a period of time, arguably AI companies have that again today. So if you can weave this into your strategy, I think you should, but you should also know when to stop.
turns.zh: 我认为停止这样做的原因在于，总会有某些类型的用户不愿意接受一对一的入职引导。在某个阶段，这些用户会变得非常重要，你需要准备好世界级的自助服务选项。当我们开始构建自助服务时，看起来几乎是不可能的。事实上，这很令人恐惧，因为很难夸大整个公司围绕手动入职理念构建的文化底蕴。毕竟，我们在一对一入职中投入了大量精力，而软件能做到的毕竟有限。现在，经过无数次的努力和坚持，我们终于做到了——如今我们拥有世界级的自助服务体验，但当时并没有做到。（00:49:49）：那么反过来想，为什么一开始要这样做呢？我们发现了两点。第一，用户指标在参与度、留存率、产品市场匹配度、月均收入（MPS）、病毒式传播等所有方面都非常出色。如果你愿意为早期客户进行一对一入职引导，你的表现将远超行业基准。当涉及到品牌建设时，拥有早期超级粉丝群体会非常有力。回想一下开头提到的对话，是什么造就了真正的病毒式传播？不是病毒机制，而是口碑传播。这才是品牌的根基。这就是你如何启动品牌建设的。（00:50:32）：第二，在一个你可以轻松快速融资的世界里，比如零利率时代，你可以用资金来避免构建首次用户体验以及所有后续必须构建的常规增长循环。相反，你可以让所有工程师专注于寻找产品市场匹配点，或深化解决方案，或拓展市场，而不是专注于首次用户体验或激活，因为有人会为你做激活工作。相比之下，我看到其他公司经常花费近一半的工程资金在这些事情上，用于构建最终未能找到产品市场匹配的自助服务流程。所以，如果你真的想打造品牌——我认为所有面向消费者的公司都需要这样做——那么如果有充足的资金（无论是过去的零利率时代，还是如今的AI公司所享有的资金），把这项工作融入你的战略中是明智之举，但你也应该知道何时适可而止。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super interesting. I guess some factors to think about, because I wanted to ask you when should people consider doing this? If they're hearing this and they're like, "This is awesome, so many problems solved if I just have somebody onboarding every new user, everyone's activated. Amazing." So some of the variables you're sharing is, do you have like cheap cash to invest in say, it doesn't have to be 20 people, it could be a few people to start. Then if there's an LTV, ACV element of just are you going to make enough from a new customer? Imagine that's a variable. Is there anything else you think founders should think about?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。我想有些因素需要考虑，因为我想问一下，人们什么时候应该考虑这样做？如果他们听到这个说法，可能会想：“太棒了，如果让专人为每个新用户做入职引导，每个人都能激活，问题就解决了。太好了。” 你分享的变量之一是，你是否有足够的资金投入。比如，不一定要20个人，开始时可以只派几个人。然后还有LTV（生命周期价值）和ACV（平均客户价值）方面的考虑——你能从新客户那里赚到足够的钱吗？想象一下这是个变量。还有其他你认为创始人应该考虑的因素吗？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Absolutely. You don't want to lose money doing this. We always made money doing onboarding to be clear, it's just that at a certain point the mass market, whether it for us it's enterprise or all of the prosumers in the world, you hit a top of funnel width, it needs to be wide enough where manually onboarding no longer makes sense.
turns.zh: 完全正确。你肯定不想在这上面亏钱。说实话，我们做用户导入（onboarding）一直都是盈利的，只不过在某个阶段，无论是面向企业级客户，还是全球的专业用户群体，市场需求都达到了峰值。此时手动导入用户的模式就失去了意义，因为市场规模必须足够大才能支撑这种增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, let's talk about product market fit. I know that everyone, when they think of Rahul, they think product market fit. You wrote this epic First Round post that described the way you guys approach product market fit. We're not going to spend a lot of time on describing it, because people can look it up. So let me just ask you this, what are a couple of things that you think people still don't understand about finding product market fit, getting to product market fit? Considering it's the most important thing you got to figure out as a founder. If you don't find something people want, nothing else matters. Anything there you want to share.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来我们来谈谈产品市场契合度。我知道一提到拉胡尔（Rahul），大家首先想到的就是产品市场契合度。你写过一篇很棒的First Round文章，详细阐述了你们团队如何寻找产品市场契合度。我们就不花太多时间复述内容了，因为大家可以自行查阅。那么我只想问你几个问题：在寻找产品市场契合度、实现产品市场契合度方面，人们还有哪些误区？毕竟这是创业者必须攻克的首要难题。如果找不到用户真正需要的产品，其他一切都无从谈起。关于这个话题，你有什么想分享的见解吗？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: The core ideas are still weird enough that I'll start there. Which is number one, you can measure product market fit. Number two, you can optimize product market fit. Number three, you can systematically, even numerically increase product market fit. And number four, you can even have an algorithm write your roadmap for you, and that is a roadmap that is guaranteed to increase product market fit. Now, if that sounds crazy, I would be the first to admit it doesn't seem like that should be true, but go check out that post. I think it is still the most widely shared post on First Round Review, it's called How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product Market Fit, or just Google the Superhuman Product Market Fit Engine. And you'll see the algorithm laid out there fully explained and why it works. (00:54:07): I'd say the second thing is to get to product market fit, you have to deliberately not act on the feedback of many of your early users. This is at the same time as listening to people intensely and building what people want. That's what we're here to do, is to make something that people want. But it can't be all people. It can't be everybody. The question becomes, how do you listen to them? And then even of what they say, what do you pay attention to and what don't you? All of that's covered in the Product Market Fit Engine.
turns.zh: 核心观点至今仍令人惊叹，我先从这四个点讲起：第一，产品市场契合度是可以衡量的；第二，产品市场契合度是可以优化的；第三，产品市场契合度可以通过系统化方法（甚至用数字化手段）来提升；第四，甚至可以让算法为你规划路线图，而且这个路线图能确保产品市场契合度不断提升。如果这听起来很疯狂，我第一个承认这看似难以置信，但大家可以去看看那篇文章。它至今仍是First Round Review上分享最广泛的文章，标题是《How Superhuman Built an Engine to Find Product Market Fit》（Superhuman如何打造产品市场契合度引擎），或者直接在谷歌上搜索“Superhuman产品市场契合度引擎”就能找到。这篇文章详细阐述了算法原理及其背后的逻辑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, I got to follow this thought on algorithmically building your roadmap to increase product market fit. Talk about how one would do that.
turns.zh: 好的，接下来我想谈谈如何通过算法构建路线图来提升产品市场契合度。具体来说，要做到两点：一是刻意忽略早期用户的反馈；二是全力倾听用户需求并按需打造产品。这正是我们作为创业者的使命——打造满足用户需求的产品。但不能面面俱到，无法满足所有人。关键在于如何倾听用户声音，以及哪些反馈值得关注，哪些则可以忽略。这些策略都在产品市场契合度引擎中有所阐述。

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Well, that's really the meat of the engine. Let's see if I can condense it here in a very easy to grok fashion. Let's assume for the sake of argument, that you can put a number on product market fit, and it turns out you can. Very simply, you're going to ask people, "How would you feel if you can no longer use this product?" You give them three responses. One of them is very disappointed, the other is somewhat disappointed, and the other is not disappointed. Very disappointed means, "I'd be devastated. I love this product. I need this product." (00:55:30): What Sean Ellis found, Sean Ellis, if you don't know him, is the guy who coined the term growth hacker, and he instrumented, benchmarked this initial question. What he found, is that the companies that struggled to grow almost always had less than 40%, very disappointed. Whereas the companies that grew the fastest almost always had more than 40%, very disappointed. And this question, this metric is way more predictive of success than something, for example, like net promoter score. (00:56:03): Okay, so far so easy. How do we make this number go up? Well, you want more people to be very disappointed without your product. The trick here is not to act too much on the feedback that the very disappointed people are giving you, because they already love your product. Also, not to act at all really on the feedback that the not disappointed people are giving, you because they're so far from loving your product that they're essentially a lost cause. But to focus on the segment of the somewhat disappointed people, they kind of love your product, but something, and I would wager something small, is holding them back. (00:56:43): You then divide them into two camps, the camp for whom the main benefit of your product resonates and the camp for whom it doesn't. What do I mean by that? Well, you go back to the people who really love your product and you basically ask them why? What is it about my products that you really love? In the early days of Superhuman, it would have been speed and keyboard shortcuts and the overall design aesthetic as well as the time that we were saving you. You then go back to the somewhat disappointed users, and in the Superhuman example, I would simply ask, "Wait, do you like Superhuman because of its speed or for something else?" And if it's something else, well, and this is hard to do, but politely disregard those people and their feedback. Because even if you built everything that they asked for, they're still pulling you in a different direction. And the thing that they like the most from your product isn't actually what the people who en mass love it the most for, is. (00:57:38): You have then articulated the subsegment of the subsegment that it makes sense to pay attention to, and there's another question in the engine to figure out what they don't like about the product. Now you have a list of things people love, you have a list of things people don't love, and you can work down that list to make the product market fit score go up. And basically at the start of every planning cycle, I advise spending half your time doubling down on what people really love and half your time systematically overcoming the objections of the somewhat disappointed users, but specifically those for whom the main benefit resonates.
turns.zh:
嗯，这才是核心要点。我看看能否用通俗易懂的方式把它简化一下。假设我们可以给产品市场匹配度打分——事实上确实可以这么做。很简单，你就问用户：“如果不能再用这款产品，你会有什么感受？”给他们三个选项。其中一个是“非常失望”，另一个是“有点失望”，第三个是“不失望”。“非常失望”意味着：“我会崩溃的。我超爱这款产品，我需要它。”（00:55:30）  
肖恩·埃利斯（Sean Ellis）发现了一个现象——如果你不了解他的话，他可是“增长黑客”这个术语的创造者——他对这个初始问题的反馈进行了数据分析。结果发现，那些难以实现增长的公司，“非常失望”的比例通常低于40%；而增长最快的公司，“非常失望”的比例则超过40%。相比之下，这个指标对成功的预测性远超诸如净推荐值之类的传统指标。（00:56:03）  
好吧，目前为止都挺简单的。那如何提升这个数字呢？关键在于要让更多用户在没有你的产品时感到“非常失望”。这里要注意的是，不要过度依赖那些“非常失望”用户的反馈，因为他们已经爱上了你的产品。同样，也不要完全忽视那些“不失望”用户的反馈，因为他们距离真正爱上你的产品还很远，基本就是“死心了”。而重点要关注那些“有点失望”的用户群体——他们对你的产品有好感，但可能被某个小问题阻碍了。（00:56:43）  
接下来，你把用户分为两类：一类是产品的主要优势能引起共鸣的，另一类则不然。怎么理解呢？回到那些真正热爱你的产品的人群，问他们为什么喜欢？Superhuman早期阶段，核心优势可能是速度、键盘快捷键、整体设计美感以及节省时间。再反问那些有点失望的用户，以Superhuman为例，你可以问：“等等，你喜欢Superhuman是因为速度还是其他原因？”如果是其他原因，那就委婉地忽略他们的反馈，因为即使你满足了他们的所有要求，他们还是会把你带向不同的方向。而他们最喜欢的产品特性，其实和大众喜爱的特性并不一致。（00:57:38）  
这样你就明确了值得关注的细分用户群体，接下来要通过另一个问题找出他们不喜欢的方面。现在你手握用户喜爱和不喜爱的清单，就可以逐项优化，提升产品市场匹配度了。基本上在每个规划周期开始时，我建议一半时间专注于强化用户喜爱之处，一半时间系统性地克服用户的顾虑，尤其是那些能与核心优势产生共鸣的群体。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That was an excellent summary. I know I said we wouldn't spend a ton of time here, but I'm really glad we did. That was really helpful. Let me ask you this, I know you used this initially in the early days, are you still operating in this way in some form?
turns.zh: 总结得非常到位。我知道我说过我们不会在这儿花太多时间，但我真的很高兴我们这么做了。这真的很有帮助。我想问一下，你最初在早期阶段使用过这个方法，现在是否还在以某种形式运作？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: We don't run the engine as is for Superhuman as a whole. There are enough subcomponents of Superhuman now that are almost individual products. For example, Superhuman for Sales, our multiplayer and collaboration features, how we think about the enterprise, AI is its whole thing, but we do sometimes run it on those individual pieces. For example, we'll ask a salesperson, the Product Market Fit Engine, as it relates to Superhuman for sales. As we think about starting new products, we would absolutely deploy the product market fit engine.
turns.zh: 我们没有将整个Superhuman的引擎原封不动地运行。目前Superhuman有足够多的子组件，几乎可以视为独立的产品。例如，面向销售的Superhuman、我们的多人协作功能，以及我们对企业客户的考量。人工智能是其核心，但我们有时会针对这些独立模块进行测试。比如，我们会向销售人员展示与销售版Superhuman相关的Product Market Fit引擎。在考虑开发新产品时，我们肯定会部署Product Market Fit引擎。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. The way you ask this question is an in-product interstitial sort of survey pop-up thing?
turns.zh: 太棒了。你提问的方式是产品内置的插页式调查弹窗之类的？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: You can do it however you want. The way Sean initially benchmarked the number was via email surveys. I think email surveys work just fine. The key thing is, and this applies to any survey methodology, if you're going to change the method of surveying, all of your old numbers are invalidated. So it's just a new baseline going forwards.
turns.zh: 你可以随心所欲地操作。Sean最初对数据的基准测试是通过邮件调查完成的。我认为邮件调查效果不错。关键在于，无论采用何种调查方法，如果你更改了调查方式，所有旧数据都将失效。所以从现在开始，新的数据将成为新的基准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. We had Sean on the podcast and he describes this method in detail. So if folks want to explore the Sean Ellis test, listen to that podcast. We'll link to it. (00:59:33): Okay, next topic that I'm excited to get your take on, is game design versus gamification. This is one of the more unique ways you think about designing product. When people hear you talk about this, they think it's like, "Oh, gamification making things like games. Oh, it's Zynga, Farmville, I don't want to do that." But you actually have a really different perspective on why you need to think about game design as you design products. Talk about your insights there.
turns.zh: 明白了。我们曾邀请Sean参加播客，他详细解释了这种方法。所以如果大家想深入了解Sean Ellis测试，可以收听那期播客。我们会附上链接。（00:59:33）：好的，接下来我想听听你对游戏设计与游戏化（gamification）的看法。这是你在产品设计中思考的独特方式之一。人们一听到“游戏化”这个词，往往会联想到“把东西做成游戏”之类的，比如Zynga的《FarmVille》之类的，但你对如何在产品设计中运用游戏设计有着截然不同的见解。能谈谈你的深刻见解吗？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Well, I strongly believe that we should make business software like we make games, because when we make products like we make games, people find them fun. They tell their friends, they fall in love with them. It's another way actually of backing into where we open this conversation, which is you're making a brand, you are giving reason for word of mouth. It's actually an altogether different kind of product development. So how do we do this? Well, as you've said, it's not gamification, that doesn't work. Game design works, but game design is not gamification. It's not, for example, simply taking your product and adding points, levels, trophies or badges. (01:00:40): To understand why gamification does not work, we actually have to start with human motivation. There's a very interesting study from Stanford that demonstrates the difference perfectly. In the 1970s, these Stanford researchers recruited children who were aged three to four years old, and all of these kids were generally pre-interested in drawing. Some kids were told they would get a reward, a certificate with a gold seal and a ribbon. And some kids were not told about any reward and they did not even expect one or didn't know of one. Now each child was then invited into a separate room to draw for six minutes and afterwards they would either get the reward or not. (01:01:21): Over the next few days, the children were observed to see how much they would continue to draw by themselves. So the children with no reward, they spent 17% of their time drawing, but the children who expected a reward, sadly they only spent 8% of their time drawing. The very presence of a reward halved their motivation. So what's happening? What's happening here, is researchers differentiate intrinsic motivation and extrinsic motivation. With intrinsic motivation we do things because they are inherently interesting and satisfying, and with extrinsic motivation, we do things to earn rewards and to achieve external goals. That's the problem with rewards, is they just massively undermine intrinsic motivation. That's why gamification doesn't work. And when gamification does work, it's because the underlying experience was already designed like a game.
turns.zh: 嗯，我坚信我们应该像制作游戏一样开发商业软件，因为当我们以游戏化的方式打造产品时，人们会觉得它们很有趣。他们会把产品推荐给朋友，甚至为之着迷。这其实也是回归到我们今天讨论的核心话题——你如何打造一个品牌，如何激发口碑传播。这实际上是一种完全不同的产品开发思路。那么该如何做到这一点呢？正如你所说，单纯的"游戏化"并不可行——游戏设计才是关键。但游戏设计不等于"游戏化"。比如说，仅仅把产品加个积分、升级等级、添加奖杯或徽章是不够的。（01:00:40）要理解为什么"游戏化"行不通，我们必须从人类动机出发。斯坦福大学的一项研究很好地揭示了其中的差异。20世纪70年代，研究人员招募了3至4岁的儿童，这些孩子普遍对绘画感兴趣。其中一些孩子被告知会获得奖励——一枚带有金色印章和丝带的证书；而另一些孩子则未被告知任何奖励，甚至不期望获得奖励。随后，每个孩子进入单独的房间进行6分钟的绘画，之后会得到或不得到奖励。（01:01:21）接下来的几天里，研究人员观察孩子们自主绘画的频率。没有奖励的孩子平均花费17%的时间绘画，而期待奖励的孩子平均只花费8%的时间绘画。奖励的存在直接削弱了他们的动机。那么问题出在哪里呢？关键在于研究者区分了内在动机和外在动机。内在动机是指人们因事物本身有趣且满足感而去做；外在动机则指人们为获取奖励或达成外部目标而行动。奖励的弊端在于，它会严重削弱内在动机。这就是游戏化行不通的原因。而当游戏化确实有效时，往往是因为底层体验本身就设计得像游戏一样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What makes something like a game? I know Superhuman is really good at this, of just your inbox zero quest that you're on. Just to make that a little more real, what is game design? What does that mean to you? What makes it feel like a game?
turns.zh: 怎样才能让某个事物像游戏一样？我知道Superhuman在这方面做得很好，比如你正在进行的收件箱清零挑战。再举个更贴近生活的例子，什么是游戏设计？它对你意味着什么？是什么让它让人感觉像游戏？

turns.speaker: Rahul Vohra
turns.en: Well, maybe folks don't know this, but before I was a founder, you can probably tell, I was actually professionally a game designer. And as it turns out, there is no unifying theory of game design. To create games, what we need to do is draw upon the arts and the science of psychology, mathematics, storytelling, interaction design. And at Superhuman we've identified five key areas that we really care about, goals, emotions, toys, controls and flow. And across these we've identified many principles of game design. One example principle would be, make fun toys and then combine those into games. (01:03:12): A question I like to ask is, are toys the same as games? They do seem different. For example, we play with toys, but we play games. A ball is a toy, but football is a game. As it turns out, the best games are constructed out of toys. Why? Because then they are fun on both levels, the toy and the game itself. So for example, in Superhuman, one of our favorite toys is the time auto-completer. If you use Superhuman, this is the thing that appears when you hit H, when you snooze or set reminders on emails. You can type whatever you want, it can be gibberish and it does its best to understand you. For example, if you type in 2D, that becomes two days, 3H is three hours, one MO is one month.
